desc:
A binary tree is complete if every level except possibly the last one is completely filled, and all nodes of the last level are as far left as possible. Equivalently, if you write the nodes level by level, left to right, there are no gaps: if the tree has n nodes they occupy exactly the positions 1..n of a heap-style numbering (the root is position 1, and the children of position i are 2i and 2i + 1).

Return true if the given tree is complete and false otherwise. The empty tree is complete.

How trees are given. There is no tree type here. A binary tree is passed as an integer array in level-order (top to bottom, left to right), the same way LeetCode serialises trees. A missing child is written as -1, and every real node value is non-negative. The children of a missing node are not listed, and trailing -1 entries are dropped, so a non-empty array never ends with -1. The empty tree is [].

For example, [1, 2, 3, -1, 4] describes the tree on the left: the root is 1 with children 2 and 3, node 2 has no left child and has 4 as its right child, and node 3 is a leaf.

    1
   / \
  2   3
   \
    4

For tree = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6] the answer is true. For tree = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, -1, 7] it is false: node 3 has a right child but no left child, so there is a gap before node 7.
constraints: Every tree array follows the encoding above exactly (valid level-order, no trailing -1)
hints: Imagine reading the tree level by level, left to right, and writing down a node or a gap for every child slot. What may never happen after the first gap?
In a complete tree all the real nodes come first and all the gaps after them. The moment you have seen one gap, no real node may follow.

Do a breadth-first walk. Keep a flag 'seen a missing child'. Whenever you meet a missing child set the flag; whenever you meet a real node while the flag is set, return false. (Alternative: number the nodes like a heap and check that the largest number equals the node count.)
editorial: Do a breadth-first traversal that also enqueues missing children as placeholders. A tree is complete exactly when, in that sequence, once a placeholder has appeared, only placeholders follow. That is the 'no gap before a real node' rule written as a state machine with one boolean.

The level-order input array is already exactly this sequence (each real node contributes its two child slots, and children of missing slots are not listed), so the scan can run directly on the array. In pointer-based form it is a standard BFS with a queue.

A second view uses heap numbering: give the root index 1 and the children of index i the indices 2i and 2i + 1. The tree is complete if and only if the largest index equals the number of nodes. Both ways take O(n) time.
